slides.label: Title
slides.notes: Open the lecture by naming the shift in viewpoint: compact Einstein geometry often uses topology, variational arguments, and global restrictions, while the non-compact setting asks for examples and constructions with much more room. The title is a report because the chapter surveys families rather than proving one single classification theorem.

slides.label: Map
slides.notes: Use this map as the organizer for the whole lecture. The left box is not a theorem; it is the change in landscape caused by giving up compactness. The three middle threads are the main constructive lenses, and the right box reminds students that every example still has to pass the same Einstein equation and completeness questions.

slides.label: Compact Contrast
slides.notes: Pause here to prevent a common misunderstanding: non-compact does not mean local or careless. Completeness, curvature bounds, and asymptotic behavior replace many closed-manifold tools. The Einstein equation is unchanged, but the global evidence that a metric is meaningful has a different shape.

slides.label: Einstein Ledger
slides.notes: This slide gives students a diagnostic checklist rather than a list of examples to memorize. Ask them to imagine a proposed metric and decide which row they would test first. The point is that the chapter’s examples become clearer when completeness, homogeneity, and the Einstein equation are not blended into one vague success criterion.

slides.label: Nonhomogeneous
slides.notes: Introduce cohomogeneity as a compromise between total symmetry and no symmetry. The diagram is deliberately schematic: the orbits are not all the same geometric size, so a transverse parameter carries real curvature information. This is why an Einstein metric built by an ansatz can be explicit without becoming homogeneous.

slides.label: ODE
slides.notes: The reduced equation is useful because it turns tensor geometry into a system one can inspect, but it also makes endpoint conditions visible. Stress that the boundary conditions encode smoothness, collapse, and completeness, not merely convenience for solving equations. This is one reason non-compact examples are delicate even when the ansatz looks elementary.

slides.label: Bundles
slides.notes: Frame bundle constructions as a way to manufacture structured non-compact spaces rather than as a separate topic. The students should see the metric as a negotiated object: the base, the fiber scale, and the connection each leave a trace in Ricci curvature. This sets up why adjusting one ingredient can restore the Einstein equation.

slides.label: Connection Curvature
slides.notes: This slide turns the bundle picture into Ricci accounting. The important teaching move is that the construction separates data at first, but the Einstein equation immediately couples it again. Students should hear that the mixed terms are not a nuisance; they are often the adjustable mechanism that makes the construction work.

slides.label: Complete Ends
slides.notes: Spend time distinguishing coordinate distance from metric distance. Many non-compact constructions live on spaces that look bounded or have visible edges in a model, but the metric can stretch those edges to infinite distance. This distinction prepares students for the bounded-domain examples, where the analytic boundary is not automatically a finite-distance boundary.

slides.label: Bounded Domains
slides.notes: Introduce bounded domains as a different engine from group actions and bundles. The construction starts from complex analysis: a potential function gives a Kähler metric, and the Einstein condition becomes an equation for that potential. The bounded picture should not mislead students, because the metric may make the analytic boundary infinitely far away.

slides.label: Kahler Einstein
slides.notes: This is the technical bridge for the bounded-domain thread. Avoid diving into proof details; instead, make the pipeline memorable. The potential gives the metric, the metric determinant gives a volume density, and the logarithmic second derivative of that density records Ricci curvature.

slides.label: Homogeneous Versus Domain
slides.notes: Use this slide to keep the chapter from fragmenting into unrelated examples. Symmetry-first and analysis-first methods look different, but they both feed into the same diagnostic questions. The comparison also helps students understand why the chapter is a report: it gathers several construction cultures around one Einstein condition.

slides.label: Failure Modes
slides.notes: This is a useful checkpoint before moving to the lab-style slides. Ask students to classify a failed construction by which test it violates first. The third failure mode is subtle: changing coordinates or reinterpreting the group action can turn an apparently new example into an old one.

slides.label: Worked Lab
slides.notes: This lab is not asking students to solve the ODE system. It asks them to read geometry from the coefficient functions. If one scale collapses and another does not, they should think about singular orbits, smoothness at the end, and curvature quantities that vary with the transverse parameter.

slides.label: Synthesis
slides.notes: This section divider is a verbal reset before the final recap. The phrase example factory is meant carefully: the non-compact setting produces many possibilities, but each possibility has to pass quality control. Ask students to name which part of the loop is supplied by symmetry, by bundle geometry, and by complex analysis.

slides.label: Recap
slides.notes: Close by tying the chapter back to the broader course. Earlier units built the Einstein equation, homogeneous examples, submersions, holonomy, and Kähler-Einstein ideas; this report shows those tools acting in a less compact world. The durable lesson is that construction methods are powerful only when paired with checks for completeness, residual curvature, and symmetry.
